**THE FIRST OF ITS KIND, SINATRA STARTED THE TREND OF ‘SUPERSTAR’ DUETS**

**GROUNDBREAKING ALBUM IS _THE_ BIGGEST WORLDWIDE SELLING DUETS ALBUM IN HISTORY**

**AVAILABLE IN THREE EDITIONS: SUPER DELUXE BOX SET, TWO-CD DELUXE EDITION, AND BEST OF DUETS SINGLE DISC COLLECTION**

**SUPER DELUXE AND TWO-CD DELUXE EDITIONS INCLUDE NEVER-BEFORE-RELEASED RECORDINGS**

_“Frank Sinatra Duets” still exudes the feeling of a hot all-star recording session. Not since the sessions in 1985 for the U.S.A. for Africa charity single “We Are the World” have so many pop superstars performed on the same record.—The New York Times, 1993_

What was referred to as “The Recording Event of the Decade,” Frank Sinatra’s groundbreaking and highly successful album Duets was originally released in November 1993, bringing together an array of global superstars, including Charles Aznavour, Anita Baker, Tony Bennett, Bono, Natalie Cole, Gloria Estefan, Aretha Franklin, Kenny G, Julio Iglesias, Liza Minnelli, Carly Simon, Barbra Streisand, and Luther Vandross for an album of standards that included many songs instantly associated with the Chairman of the Board.

To commemorate the 20th Anniversary of the groundbreaking, multi-platinum selling album, Capitol/UMe will release [Frank Sinatra: Sinatra Duets – Twentieth Anniversary](http://smarturl.it/SinatraDuetsSuperDlx), on November 19, 2013, bringing together the original Duets and the follow-up Duets II, together in one deluxe package. Frank Sinatra: Sinatra Duets – Twentieth Anniversary will be available in three editions:

• [Super Deluxe Box Set](http://smarturl.it/SinatraDuetsSuperDlx) featuring Duets and Duets II 180-gram vinyl records in a gatefold LP jacket, two CDs including Duets and Duets II with bonus and unreleased tracks, a standard DVD featuring interviews, the official EPK and a promo video of “I’ve Got You Under My Skin” duet with Bono, plus a 20-page LP sized booklet with rare photos and new liner notes, an embossed lithograph with envelope, all housed in an elegant 12”x12” box complete with a gold foil-stamped title.

• [Two-CD Deluxe Edition](http://smarturl.it/SinatraDuetsDeluxe) with bonus and unreleased tracks and a 32-page booklet with rare photos and new liner notes.

• [Two-LP vinyl version](http://smarturl.it/SinatraDuetsVinyl) of the original Duets and Duets II releases on 180-gram vinyl, gatefold jacket.

[The Super Deluxe Edition](http://smarturl.it/SinatraDuetsSuperDlx) and [2-CD Deluxe Edition](http://smarturl.it/SinatraDuetsDeluxe) releases will include two never-before-released recordings, “One for My Baby (And One More for the Road)” featuring Tom Scott and “Embraceable You” with Tanya Tucker, plus the rare bonus tracks “Fly Me to the Moon” with George Strait, and two versions of “My Way,” one recorded with Luciano Pavarotti and the other with Willie Nelson.

In addition to these three anniversary editions, Capitol/Ume will also release [Best Of Duets](http://smarturl.it/BestOfDuets), a 14-song, single-disc collection featuring key tracks from both Duets and Duets II and the bonus track “My Way” featuring Luciano Pavarotti.

Sinatra recorded his tracks “live” with a 54-piece orchestra at the Capitol studios, the way he originally recorded his classic Capitol albums. In a pioneering move for the recording industry, at various locations using digital technology, Sinatra’s ‘duet’ partners recorded their own vocal tracks to his recordings, allowing them to virtually ‘duet’ with one of the greatest entertainers of all time. Duets made history, not only for its cutting edge recording techniques, and having a renowned contemporary artist, LeRoy Neiman, specially commissioned for album artwork, but for being one of the most successful selling albums of the year, with the album shipping more than 1.3 million units and putting the 77-year-old Sinatra at the No. 2 spot on the _Billboard_ charts, between Pearl Jam’s Vs. and Meatloaf’s Bat Out Of Hell II.

The highly successful follow-up, Duets II, was released the following year and included Jimmy Buffett, Neil Diamond, Lena Horne, Chrissie Hynde, Antonio Carlos Jobim, Patti LaBelle, Steve Lawrence & Eydie Gorme, Luis Miguel, Lorrie Morgan, Willie Nelson, Linda Ronstadt, Jon Secada, Frank Sinatra Jr., Stevie Wonder & Gladys Knight. Once again, Sinatra enjoyed a multiplatinum Top 10 record on the charts with Duets II at No. 9 on _Billboard_’s Top 200 Chart.

Even after 50 years of recording, Sinatra continued to blaze a trail for artists and once again cut across all musical genres. These unique recordings are tributes to his legacy and to the immeasurable impact and influence he continues to have on music today.

# The Taylor Swift Holiday Collection - EP

[Taylor Swift](https://music.apple.com/us/artist/taylor-swift/159260351)

Holiday · 2007

Taylor Swift's six-song Holiday EP is a class act. Originally released in October 2007 as an exclusive-only available at participating Target stores in America, _The Taylor Swift Holiday Collection_ was re-released for wider distribution in December 2008. Rather than open with a traditional carol, Swift starts the party with a playful version of "Last Christmas," originally penned by George Michael as a double a-sided 45 rpm single for his British pop duo Wham! in 1984. Christmas bells and banjos replace synthesizers and falsettos making for a fitting update. She gets more pensive and lovelorn on the following acoustic ballad "Christmases When You Were Mine," one of two songs here that she had a hand in writing. "Santa Baby" gets twanged up and sung with a girlish tone that comes off more innocent than the flirty versions by Eartha Kitt and Madonna. Swift changes Franz Xaver Gruber's 1863 melody on a breathtaking version of "Silent Night," leaving Josef Mohr's lyrics intact making for what sounds like a brand new, but familiar, song. "Christmas Must Be Something More" is a holiday hit. Her sole original here, the song bounces with the youthful exuberance and barbed hooks that Swift excels at writing and singing.

Beach](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/viola-beach-mn0003472410 "Viola Beach") ## [Blossoms Biography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/blossoms-mn0003457444\#biography "Blossoms Biography") ### Blossoms Biography by [Neil Z. Yeung](https://www.allmusic.com/author/neil-z-yeung "View more by Neil Z. Yeung") [![Cool Like You](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0004867556/front/220/-hxcWU6FL41wvd-OXa0Ypd_M69_UI9rrJSVvWL2-yAg=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/cool-like-you-mw0003159621 "Cool Like You") English quintet Blossoms burst onto the British scene in the 2010s, quickly rising from local clubs to festival stages within a few short years. Their breakthrough debut landed in 2016 after years of anticipation, topping charts and winning fans with a catchy, synth-forward blend of Brit-pop and indie rock heard on songs like hit single "Charlemagne." Incorporating more new wave influences on their follow-up, 2018's [Cool Like You](https://www.allmusic.com/album/cool-like-you-mw0003159621), the band maintained their presence on U.K. charts and on the touring circuit. By the end of the decade, they were selling out shows, including one at a hometown stadium. The group entered a new decade in 2020 with their third LP, the lovelorn [Foolish Loving Spaces](https://www.allmusic.com/album/foolish-loving-spaces-mw0003338258). They soon followed with 2022's [Ribbon Around the Bomb](https://www.allmusic.com/album/ribbon-around-the-bomb-mw0003660277). Formed in Stockport by school chums [Tom Ogden](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/tom-ogden-mn0003422968) (vocals, guitar) and [Joe Donovan](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/joe-donovan-mn0003506047) (drums), Blossoms later incorporated [Charlie Salt](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/charlie-salt-mn0003422909) (bass, vocals), [Josh Dewhurst](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/josh-dewhurst-mn0003422937) (guitar), and [Myles Kellock](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/myles-kellock-mn0003422955) (keyboards, vocals) to round out their lineup. Their sound was pigeonholed as psych-pop, which the band didn't like; rather, they hit a sweet spot between [the Doors](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-doors-mn0000114342) and [Arctic Monkeys](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/arctic-monkeys-mn0000325357), combining a knack for classic pop songwriting and moody organ atmospherics with a youthful energy. [Ogden](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/ogden-mn0003422968)'s delivery occupied the space between [Richard Ashcroft](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/richard-ashcroft-mn0000290853) ( [the Verve](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-verve-mn0000575522)) and [Alex Turner](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/alex-turner-mn0000934227), of the aforementioned [Monkeys](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/monkeys-mn0000325357), as the group slithered from spooky, groovy warmth to peppy Brit-pop. Debut single "You Pulled a Gun on Me" was a fine example of this combination, and the band continued to develop on subsequent singles "Blow" and "Cut Me and I'll Bleed." [![Blown Rose EP](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0004445643/front/220/JXu5WjPPLXdQVrLs-fzCTD6KsMttLlyBmmVTZ6_CLs0=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/blown-rose-ep-mw0002867126 "Blown Rose EP") 2015 saw the release of two EPs -- [Blown Rose](https://www.allmusic.com/album/blown-rose-mw0002867126) and [Charlemagne](https://www.allmusic.com/album/charlemagne-mw0002892503). As Blossoms gained exposure, they released another EP, [At Most a Kiss](https://www.allmusic.com/album/at-most-a-kiss-mw0002907380), in February 2016. The four-song set featured some new elements in the band's sound, including prominent synths and a more driving urgency. A month later, the group revealed plans for their debut full-length. The self-titled [Blossoms](https://www.allmusic.com/album/blossoms-mw0002947404) was released in summer 2016, topping U.K. and Scottish charts. Months later, they bolstered the effort with an extended edition that included ten additional songs. [![In Isolation](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0005242001/front/220/CFduE_ICs2WchbyaiDEM3phUoDg0hsvx4F4sL4oO-nA=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/in-isolation-mw0003403967 "In Isolation") In early 2018, Blossoms issued the singles "I Can't Stand It" and "There's a Reason Why (I Never Returned Your Calls)," which both appeared on their sophomore effort, [Cool Like You](https://www.allmusic.com/album/cool-like-you-mw0003159621), an even more pop-leaning record that arrived in April. The band continued to build a devoted fan base, selling out shows across the country. Their third LP arrived in January 2020. Titled [Foolish Loving Spaces](https://www.allmusic.com/album/foolish-loving-spaces-mw0003338258), the project's lyrical focus centered on themes of love and attachment, adopting a sound inspired by [Talking Heads](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/talking-heads-mn0000131650) and [U2](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/u2-mn0000219203), and gave them their second U.K. chart-topper. 2020's COVID-19 lockdown saw the band digitally release the remotely recorded [In Isolation](https://www.allmusic.com/album/in-isolation-mw0003403967), a stop-gap which included reworkings of some of their own songs and covers of tunes by [Babybird](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/babybird-mn0000073668), [Elvis Costello](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/elvis-costello-mn0000058549), and [the Beatles](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-beatles-mn0000754032), and a recording of a show [Live from the Plaza Theatre, Stockport](https://www.allmusic.com/album/live-from-the-plaza-theatre-stockport-mw0003407695); the two were bundled together for a physical release. 2022 brought Blossoms' fourth studio album, [Ribbon Around the Bomb](https://www.allmusic.com/album/ribbon-around-the-bomb-mw0003660277), which saw a slight return to their early-'60s-inspired sound, with shades of [Procol Harum](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/procol-harum-mn0000304401). In 2023, the group teamed up with '80s chart-topper [Rick Astley](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/rick-astley-mn0000354722) for a set of live shows performing covers of legendary English rock outfit [The Smiths](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-smiths-mn0000899530), culminating in an appearance at Glastonbury festival that summer. In 2024, the group began the roll-out for their fifth studio album, [Gary](https://www.allmusic.com/album/gary-mw0004308021), named after a fiberglass gorilla statue stolen from a garden center in Scotland. With production and writing from [Josh Lloyd-Watson](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/josh-lloyd-watson-mn0003236807) ( [Jungle](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/jungle-mn0003229446)), [James Skelly](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/james-skelly-mn0002162673) ( [the Coral](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-coral-mn0000061041)), and [CMAT](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cmat-mn0004150353), the group's 2024 LP landed them atop the U.K. album charts once again. ## [Blossoms Discography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/blossoms-mn0003457444\#discography "Blossoms Discography") Main AlbumsCompilationsSingles & EPsAll Year (Oldest to Newest)Year (Newest to Oldest)AllMusic Rating (Highest to Lowest)AllMusic Rating (Lowest to Highest)User Ratings (Highest to Lowest)User Ratings (Lowest to Highest)Album Title (A-Z)Album Title (Z-A) | | Year | Credit | AllMusic Rating | User Rating | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [![Blossoms](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0004571927/front/120/yCrCi_vmXYrqd-ZBx7-hVphUoDg0hsvx4F4sL4oO-nA=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/blossoms-mw0002947404 "Blossoms") | 2016 | [Blossoms](https://www.allmusic.com/album/blossoms-mw0002947404 "Blossoms")

## [Frank Sinatra Biography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/frank-sinatra-mn0000792507\#biography "Frank Sinatra Biography")

### Frank Sinatra Biography  by   [William Ruhlmann](https://www.allmusic.com/author/william-ruhlmann "View more by William Ruhlmann")

Frank Sinatra was arguably the most important musical figure of the 20th century, his only real rivals for the title being [Elvis Presley](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/elvis-presley-mn0000180228) and [the Beatles](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-beatles-mn0000754032). In a professional career lasting 60 years, he demonstrated a remarkable ability to maintain his appeal and pursue his musical goals despite countervailing trends. He came to the fore during the swing era of the 1930s and '40s, helped to define the "sing era" of the '40s and '50s, and continued to attract listeners during the rock era that began in the mid-'50s. He scored his first number one hit in 1940 and was still making million-selling recordings in 1994. This popularity was a mark of his success at singing and promoting the American popular song as it was written, particularly in the 1920s, '30s, and '40s. He was able to take the work of great theater composers of that period, such as [Jerome Kern](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/jerome-kern-mn0000031646), [Irving Berlin](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/irving-berlin-mn0000103748), [George Gershwin](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/george-gershwin-mn0000197918), [Cole Porter](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cole-porter-mn0000109607), and [Richard Rodgers](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/richard-rodgers-mn0000820913), and reinterpret their songs for later audiences in a way that led to their rediscovery and their permanent enshrinement as classics. On records and in live performances, on film, radio, and television, he consistently sang standards in a way that demonstrated their perennial appeal.

The son of a fireman, Sinatra dropped out of high school in his senior year to pursue a career in music. In September 1935, he appeared as part of the vocal group the Hoboken Four on Major Bowes' Original Amateur Hour. The group won the radio show contest and toured with Bowes. Sinatra then took a job as a singing waiter and MC at the Rustic Cabin in Englewood, NJ. He was still singing there in the spring of 1939, when he was heard over the radio by trumpeter [Harry James](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/harry-james-mn0000950571), who had recently organized his own big band after leaving [Benny Goodman](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/benny-goodman-mn0000163133). [James](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/james-mn0000950571) hired Sinatra, and the new singer made his first recordings on July 13, 1939. At the end of the year, Sinatra accepted an offer from the far more successful bandleader [Tommy Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/tommy-dorsey-mn0000934072), jumping to his new berth in January 1940. Over the next two and a half years, he was featured on 16 Top Ten hits recorded by [Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/dorsey-mn0000934072), among them the chart-topper "I'll Never Smile Again," later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. During this period, he also performed on various radio shows with [Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/dorsey-mn0000934072) and appeared with the band in the films Las Vegas Nights (1941) and Ship Ahoy (1942).

In January 1942, he tested the waters for a solo career by recording a four-song session arranged and conducted by [Axel Stordahl](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/axel-stordahl-mn0000307225) that included [Cole Porter](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cole-porter-mn0000109607)'s "Night and Day," which became his first chart entry under his own name in March 1942. Soon after, he gave [Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/dorsey-mn0000934072) notice. Sinatra left the [Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/dorsey-mn0000934072) band in September 1942. The recording ban called by the American Federation of Musicians, which had begun the previous month, initially prevented him from making records, but he appeared on a 15-minute radio series, Songs By Sinatra, from October through the end of the year and also did a few live dates. His big breakthrough came due to his engagement as a support act to [Benny Goodman](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/benny-goodman-mn0000163133) at the Paramount Theatre in New York, which began on New Year's Eve. It made him a popular phenomenon, the first real teen idol, with school girls swooning in the aisles. RCA Victor, which had been doling out stockpiled [Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/dorsey-mn0000934072) recordings during the strike, scored with "There Are Such Things," which had a Sinatra vocal; it hit number one in January 1943, as did "In the Blue of the Evening," another [Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/dorsey-mn0000934072) record featuring Sinatra, in August, while a third [Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/dorsey-mn0000934072)/Sinatra release, "It's Always You," hit the Top Five later in the year, and a fourth, "I'll Be Seeing You," reached the Top Ten in 1944. Columbia, which controlled the [Harry James](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/harry-james-mn0000950571) recordings, reissued the four-year-old "All or Nothing at All," re-billed as being by Frank Sinatra with [Harry James & His Orchestra](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/harry-james-his-orchestra-mn0000666331), and it hit number one in September. Meanwhile, the label had signed Sinatra as a solo artist, and in a temporary loophole to the recording ban, put him in the studio to record a cappella, backed only by a vocal chorus. This resulted in four Top Ten hits in 1943, among them "People Will Say We're in Love" from [Richard Rodgers](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/richard-rodgers-mn0000820913) and [Oscar Hammerstein II](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/oscar-hammerstein-ii-mn0000804858)'s musical Oklahoma!, and a fifth in early 1944 ("I Couldn't Sleep a Wink Last Night") before protests from the musicians union ended a cappella recording.

In February 1943, Sinatra was hired by the popular radio series Your Hit Parade, on which he performed through the end of 1944. Adding to his radio duties, he appeared from June through October on Broadway Bandbox and in the fall again took up the Songs by Sinatra show, which ran through December. In January, it was expanded to a half-hour as The Frank Sinatra Show, which ran for a year and a half. In April 1943, he made his first credited appearance in a motion picture, singing "Night and Day" in Reveille with Beverly. This was followed by Higher and Higher, released in December, in which he had a small acting role, playing himself, and by Step Lively, released in July 1944, which gave him a larger part. MGM was sufficiently impressed by these performances to put him under contract. The recording ban was lifted in November 1944, and Sinatra returned to making records, beginning with a cover of [Irving Berlin](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/irving-berlin-mn0000103748)'s "White Christmas" that was in the Top Ten before the end of the year. Among his eight recordings to peak in the Top Ten in 1945 were [Jule Styne](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/jule-styne-mn0000304458) and [Sammy Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/sammy-cahn-mn0000987625)'s "Saturday Night (Is the Loneliest Night of the Week)," [Johnny Mercer](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/johnny-mercer-mn0000244406)'s "Dream," [Styne](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/styne-mn0000304458) and [Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cahn-mn0000987625)'s "I Should Care," and "If I Loved You" and "You'll Never Walk Alone" from the [Rodgers & Hammerstein](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/rodgers-hammerstein-mn0000245385) musical Carousel. Sinatra insisted that [Styne](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/styne-mn0000304458) and [Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cahn-mn0000987625) be hired to write the songs for his first MGM musical, Anchors Aweigh, and over the course of his career, the singer recorded more songs by [Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cahn-mn0000987625) (a lyricist who worked with several composers) than by any other songwriter. Anchors Aweigh, in which Sinatra was paired with [Gene Kelly](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/gene-kelly-mn0000802791), was released in July 1945 and went on to become the most successful film of the year.

[![The Voice of Frank Sinatra](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0000833329/front/220/Q28zAP7FlcmcNuPQcz281hyhM-OFI8zG4l-qVpXXB1I=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-voice-of-frank-sinatra-mw0000659223 "The Voice of Frank Sinatra")
Sinatra returned to radio in September with a new show bearing an old name, Songs by Sinatra. It ran weekly for the next two seasons, concluding in June 1947. Among his eight Top Ten hits in 1946 were two that hit number one ("Oh! What It Seemed to Be" and [Styne](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/styne-mn0000304458) and [Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cahn-mn0000987625)'s "Five Minutes More"), as well as "They Say It's Wonderful" and "The Girl That I Marry" from [Irving Berlin](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/irving-berlin-mn0000103748)'s musical Annie Get Your Gun, [Jerome Kern](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/jerome-kern-mn0000031646)'s "All Through the Day," and [Kurt Weill](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/kurt-weill-mn0000683446)'s "September Song." He also topped the album charts with the collection [The Voice of Frank Sinatra](https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-voice-of-frank-sinatra-mw0000659223). His only film appearance for the year came in [Till the Clouds Roll By](https://www.allmusic.com/album/till-the-clouds-roll-by-mw0000104112), a biography of the recently deceased [Kern](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/kern-mn0000031646), in which he sang "Ol' Man River."

[![Songs by Sinatra](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0001515129/front/220/TQVQrse-KCE1iMTanMMJV9_M69_UI9rrJSVvWL2-yAg=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/songs-by-sinatra-mw0000849558 "Songs by Sinatra")
By 1947, Sinatra's early success had crested, though he continued to work steadily in several media. On radio, he returned to the cast of Your Hit Parade in September 1947, appearing on the series for the next two seasons, then had his own 15-minute show, Light-Up Time, during 1949-1950. On film, he appeared in five more movies through the end of the decade, including both big-budget MGM musicals like On the Town and minor efforts such as The Kissing Bandit. He scored eight Top Ten hits in 1947-1949, including "Mam'selle," which hit number one in May 1947, and "Some Enchanted Evening," from the [Rodgers & Hammerstein](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/rodgers-hammerstein-mn0000245385) musical South Pacific. He also hit the Top Ten of the album charts with 1947's [Songs by Sinatra](https://www.allmusic.com/album/songs-by-sinatra-mw0000849558) and 1948's [Christmas Songs by Sinatra](https://www.allmusic.com/album/christmas-songs-by-sinatra-mw0000120603). Sinatra's career was in decline by the start of the '50s, but he was far from inactive. He entered the fall of 1950 with both a new radio show and his first venture into television. On radio, there was Meet Frank Sinatra, which found the singer acting as a disc jockey; it ran through the end of the season. On TV, there was The Frank Sinatra Show, a musical-variety series; it lasted until April 1952. His film work had nearly subsided, though in March 1952 came the drama Meet Danny Wilson, which tested his acting abilities and gave him the opportunity to sing such songs as [Harold Arlen](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/harold-arlen-mn0000060306) and [Johnny Mercer](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/johnny-mercer-mn0000244406)'s "That Old Black Magic," "I've Got a Crush on You" by [George](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/george-mn0000771470) and [Ira Gershwin](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/ira-gershwin-mn0000200301), and "How Deep Is the Ocean?" by [Irving Berlin](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/irving-berlin-mn0000103748).

At Columbia Records, Sinatra came into increasing conflict with musical director [Mitch Miller](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/mitch-miller-mn0000577261), who was finding success for his singers by using novelty material and gimmicky arrangements. Sinatra resisted this approach, and though he managed to score four more Top Ten hits during 1950-1951 -- among them an unlikely reading of the folk standard "Goodnight Irene" -- he and Columbia parted ways. Thus, ten years after launching his solo career, he ended 1952 without a record, film, radio, or television contract. Then he turned it all around. The first step was recording. Sinatra agreed to a long-term, boilerplate contract with Capitol Records, which had been co-founded by [Johnny Mercer](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/johnny-mercer-mn0000244406) a decade earlier and had a roster full of faded '40s performers. In June 1953, he scored his first Top Ten hit in a year and a half with "I'm Walking Behind You." Then in August, he returned to film, playing a non-singing, featured role in the World War II drama [From Here to Eternity](https://www.allmusic.com/album/from-here-to-eternity-mw0002148548), a performance that earned respect for his acting abilities, to the extent that he won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for the part on March 25, 1954. In the fall of 1953, Sinatra began two new radio series: Rocky Fortune, a drama on which he played a detective, ran from October to March 1954; and The Frank Sinatra Show was a 15-minute, twice-a-week music series that ran for two seasons, concluding in July 1955.

[![Songs for Young Lovers](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0004448027/front/220/E7hRAyKlpJpl5uV7JxgUah_TZlp6n_cq-Emr2zx15tU=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/songs-for-young-lovers-mw0000851214 "Songs for Young Lovers")
Meanwhile, Sinatra had begun working with arranger/conductor [Nelson Riddle](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/nelson-riddle-mn0000322027), a pairing that produced notable chart entries in February 1954 on both the singles and albums charts. "Young-at-Heart," which just missed hitting number one, was the singer's biggest single since 1947, and the song went on to become a standard. (The title was used for a 1955 movie in which Sinatra starred.) Then there was the 10" LP [Songs for Young Lovers](https://www.allmusic.com/album/songs-for-young-lovers-mw0000851214), the first of Sinatra's "concept" albums, on which he and [Riddle](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/riddle-mn0000322027) revisited classic songs by [Cole Porter](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cole-porter-mn0000109607), the Gershwins, and [Rodgers](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/rodgers-mn0001168733) and [Hart](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/hart-mn0000209620) in contemporary arrangements with vocal interpretations that conveyed the wit and grace of the lyrics. The album lodged in the Top Five. In July, Sinatra had another Top Ten single with [Styne](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/styne-mn0000304458) and [Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cahn-mn0000987625)'s "Three Coins in the Fountain," and in September [Swing Easy!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/swing-easy%21-mw0000849204) matched the success of its predecessor on the LP chart. By the middle of the '50s, Sinatra had reclaimed his place as a star singer and actor; in fact, he had taken a more prominent place than he had had in the heady days of the mid-'40s. In 1955, he hit number one with the single "Learnin' the Blues" and the 12" LP [In the Wee Small Hours](https://www.allmusic.com/album/in-the-wee-small-hours-mw0000650776), a ballad collection later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

[![Songs for Swingin' Lovers!](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0000828133/front/220/wj4am3AKO1Ey84kXO6mnvlWnbEN5fCjifro6xhIBuB4=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/songs-for-swingin-lovers%21-mw0000195713 "Songs for Swingin' Lovers!")
On September 15, 1955, he appeared in a television production of Our Town and sang "Love and Marriage" (specially written by [Sammy Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/sammy-cahn-mn0000987625) and his new partner [James Van Heusen](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/james-van-heusen-mn0000309464)), which became a Top Five hit. Early in 1956, he was back in the Top Ten with [Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cahn-mn0000987625) and [Van Heusen](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/van-heusen-mn0000309464)'s "(Love Is) The Tender Trap," the theme song from his new film, The Tender Trap. As part of his thematic concepts for his albums of the '50s, Sinatra alternated between records devoted to slow arrangements ( [In the Wee Small Hours](https://www.allmusic.com/album/in-the-wee-small-hours-mw0000650776)) and those given over to dance charts ( [Swing Easy](https://www.allmusic.com/album/swing-easy-mw0000849204)). By the late winter of 1956, the schedule called for another dance album, and [Songs for Swingin' Lovers!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/songs-for-swingin-lovers%21-mw0000195713), released in March, filled the bill, stopping just short of number one and going gold. The rise of rock & roll and [Elvis Presley](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/elvis-presley-mn0000180228) began to make the singles charts the almost-exclusive province of teen idols, but Sinatra's "Hey! Jealous Lover" (by [Sammy Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/sammy-cahn-mn0000987625), [Kay Twomey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/kay-twomey-mn0000309936), and [Bee Walker](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/bee-walker-mn0000149849)), released in October, gave him another Top Five hit in 1957. Meanwhile, he ruled the LP charts. The Capitol singles compilation [This Is Sinatra!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/this-is-sinatra%21-mw0000847168), released in November, hit the Top Ten and went gold.

[![Close to You and More](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0000828274/front/220/pNV1_Pwv1Zt-qESY8y4zth_TZlp6n_cq-Emr2zx15tU=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/close-to-you-and-more-mw0000191733 "Close to You and More")
Sinatra began 1957 by releasing [Close to You](https://www.allmusic.com/album/close-to-you-mw0000191733), a ballad album with accompaniment by a string quartet, in February. It hit the Top Five, followed in May by [A Swingin' Affair!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/a-swingin-affair%21-mw0000312463), which went to number one, and another ballad album, [Where Are You?](https://www.allmusic.com/album/where-are-you--mw0000691401), a Top Five hit after release in September. He was also represented in the LP charts in November by the soundtrack to his film Pal Joey (based on a [Rodgers & Hart](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/rodgers-hart-mn0000843194) musical), which hit the Top Five, and by the seasonal collection [A Jolly Christmas From Frank Sinatra](https://www.allmusic.com/album/a-jolly-christmas-from-frank-sinatra-mw0000193934), which eventually was certified platinum. The Joker Is Wild, another of his 1957 films, featured the [Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cahn-mn0000987625)- [Van Heusen](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/van-heusen-mn0000309464) song "All the Way," which became a Top Five single. In October, he returned to prime time television with another series called The Frank Sinatra Show, but it lasted only one season, and subsequently he restricted his TV appearances largely to specials (of which he made many).

[![Come Fly with Me](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0000446151/front/220/aCo3H7BeFsL-Em9xrvVjeR_TZlp6n_cq-Emr2zx15tU=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/come-fly-with-me-mw0000194130 "Come Fly with Me")
In February 1958, Sinatra reached the Top Ten with "Witchcraft," his last single to perform that well for the next eight years. That month, Capitol released [Come Fly with Me](https://www.allmusic.com/album/come-fly-with-me-mw0000194130), a travel-themed rhythm album, which hit number one. The year's ballad album, [Frank Sinatra Sings for Only the Lonely](https://www.allmusic.com/album/frank-sinatra-sings-for-only-the-lonely-mw0000194131), released in September, also topped the charts, and it went gold. In between, Capitol released the compilation [This Is Sinatra, Vol. 2](https://www.allmusic.com/album/this-is-sinatra-vol-2-mw0000319369), which hit the Top Ten. 1959 followed a similar pattern. [Come Dance with Me!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/come-dance-with-me%21-mw0000651533) appeared in January and became a gold-selling Top Ten hit. It also won Sinatra Grammy Awards for Album of the Year and for vocal performance. [Look to Your Heart](https://www.allmusic.com/album/look-to-your-heart-mw0000850680), a compilation, was released in the spring and reached the Top Ten. And [No One Cares](https://www.allmusic.com/album/no-one-cares-mw0000312462), the year's ballad collection, appeared in the summer and just missed topping the charts.

[![Sinatra's Swingin' Session!!! And More](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0001461867/front/220/7LtClY9PXlXj2S0Gx0EqxYAf7E_1E-2MlBBPmPAXRBU=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatras-swingin-session%21%21%21-and-more-mw0000191853 "Sinatra's Swingin' Session!!! And More")
Sinatra gradually did less singing in his movies of the '50s, but in March 1960, he appeared in a movie version of [Cole Porter](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cole-porter-mn0000109607)'s musical Can-Can, and the resulting soundtrack album hit the Top Ten. Meanwhile, Sinatra was beginning to think about the approaching end of his Capitol Records contract and to enter the studio less frequently for the company. His next regular album was a year in coming, and when it did, [Nice 'n' Easy](https://www.allmusic.com/album/nice-n-easy-mw0000962864) was a mid-tempo collection, breaking his pattern of alternating fast and slow albums. The wait may have caused pent-up demand; the album spent many weeks at number one and went gold. Although Sinatra had not yet completed his recording commitment to Capitol, he began in December 1960 to make recordings for his own label, which he called Reprise Records. As a result, record stores were deluged with five new Sinatra albums in 1961: in January, Capitol had [Sinatra's Swingin' Session!!!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatras-swingin-session%21%21%21-mw0000191853); in April, Reprise was launched with the release of [Ring-a-Ding Ding!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/ring-a-ding-ding%21-mw0000272901); in July, Reprise followed with Sinatra Swings the same week that Capitol released [Come Swing with Me!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/come-swing-with-me%21-mw0000691398); and in October, Reprise had [I Remember Tommy...](https://www.allmusic.com/album/i-remember-tommy-mw0000097922), an album of songs Sinatra had sung with the [Tommy Dorsey](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/tommy-dorsey-mn0000934072) band. There was also the March compilation [All the Way](https://www.allmusic.com/album/all-the-way-mw0000079980) on Capitol, making for six releases in one year. Remarkably, they all reached the Top Ten.

[![Point of No Return](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0001120128/front/220/Xzfme0qJWsiI0IXWu0YWDxyhM-OFI8zG4l-qVpXXB1I=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/point-of-no-return-mw0000198053 "Point of No Return")
Meanwhile, Reprise's first single, "The Second Time Around," a song written by [Cahn](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/cahn-mn0000987625) and [Van Heusen](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/van-heusen-mn0000309464) for [Bing Crosby](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/bing-crosby-mn0000094252), won Sinatra the Grammy for Record of the Year. By 1962, the market was glutted. Capitol released its last new Sinatra album, [Point of No Return](https://www.allmusic.com/album/point-of-no-return-mw0000198053), as well as a compilation, and Reprise put out three new LPs, but only Reprise's [Sinatra & Strings](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatra-strings-mw0000676504) reached the Top Ten. In 1963, however, all three Reprise releases, [Sinatra-Basie](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatra-basie-mw0000195377), [The Concert Sinatra](https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-concert-sinatra-mw0000191854), and the gold-selling [Sinatra's Sinatra](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatras-sinatra-mw0000311932), made the Top Ten. The onset of [the Beatles](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-beatles-mn0000754032) in 1964 began to do to the LP charts what [Elvis Presley](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/elvis-presley-mn0000180228) had done to the singles charts in 1956, but Sinatra continued to reach the Top Ten with his albums of the mid-'60s, albeit not as consistently. [Days of Wine and Roses, Moon River, and Other Academy Award Winners](https://www.allmusic.com/album/days-of-wine-and-roses-moon-river-and-other-academy-award-winners-mw0000201386) hit that ranking in May 1964, as did [Sinatra '65](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatra-65-mw0000849150) in August 1965. That same month, Sinatra mounted a commercial comeback by emphasizing his own advancing age. Nearing 50, he released [September of My Years](https://www.allmusic.com/album/september-of-my-years-mw0000191734), a ballad collection keyed to the passage of time. After "It Was a Very Good Year" was drawn from the album as a single and rose into the Top 40, the LP took off for the Top Five and went gold. It was named 1965 Album of the Year at the Grammy Awards, and Sinatra also picked up a trophy for best vocal performance for "It Was a Very Good Year."

[![Sinatra at the Sands](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0000282234/front/220/jyQYGwzCIQfsRhD0pbJTc4Af7E_1E-2MlBBPmPAXRBU=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatra-at-the-sands-mw0000650777 "Sinatra at the Sands")
In November 1965, Sinatra starred in a retrospective TV special, A Man and His Music, and released a corresponding double-LP, which reached the Top Ten and went gold. It won the 1966 Grammy for Album of the Year. Sinatra returned to number one on the singles charts for the first time in 11 years with the million-selling "Strangers in the Night" in July 1966; the song won him Grammys for Record of the Year and best vocal performance. A follow-up album named after the single topped the LP charts and went platinum. Before the end of the year, Sinatra had released two more Top Ten, gold-selling albums, [Sinatra at the Sands](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatra-at-the-sands-mw0000650777) and [That's Life](https://www.allmusic.com/album/thats-life-mw0000120391), the latter anchored by the title song, a Top Five single. In April 1967, Sinatra was back at number one on the singles charts with the million-selling "Somethin' Stupid," a duet with his daughter [Nancy](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/nancy-mn0000366043). By the late '60s, even Sinatra had trouble resisting the succeeding waves of youth-oriented rock music that topped the charts. But [Frank Sinatra's Greatest Hits!](https://www.allmusic.com/album/frank-sinatras-greatest-hits%21-mw0000728530), a compilation of his '60s singles successes released in August 1968, was a million-seller, and [Cycles](https://www.allmusic.com/album/cycles-mw0000268470), an album of songs by contemporary writers like [Joni Mitchell](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/joni-mitchell-mn0000270491) and [Jimmy Webb](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/jimmy-webb-mn0000129761), released that fall, went gold.

[![Ol' Blue Eyes Is Back](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0001379208/front/220/dHSsUllSJjhrwdY9PvZHJD6KsMttLlyBmmVTZ6_CLs0=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/ol-blue-eyes-is-back-mw0000195712 "Ol' Blue Eyes Is Back")
In March 1969, Sinatra released "My Way," with a lyric specially crafted for him by [Paul Anka](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/paul-anka-mn0000745915). It quickly became a signature song for him. The single reached the Top 40, and an album of the same name hit the Top Ten and went gold. In the spring of 1971, at the age of 55, Sinatra announced his retirement. But he remained retired only until the fall of 1973, when he returned to action with a new gold-selling album and a TV special both called [Ol' Blue Eyes Is Back](https://www.allmusic.com/album/ol-blue-eyes-is-back-mw0000195712). In this late phase of his career, Sinatra cut back on records, movies, and television in favor of live performing, particularly in Las Vegas, but also in concert halls, arenas, and stadiums around the world. He refrained from making any new studio albums for six years, then returned in March 1980 with a three-LP set, [Trilogy: Past, Present, Future](https://www.allmusic.com/album/trilogy-past-present-future-mw0000197932). The most memorable track from the gold-selling set turned out to be "Theme From New York, New York," the title song from the 1977 movie, which Sinatra's recording belatedly turned into a standard.

[![Sinatra Reprise: The Very Good Years](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0001216717/front/220/ozBkZj-7pAoJjGlFrn-9k5hUoDg0hsvx4F4sL4oO-nA=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatra-reprise-the-very-good-years-mw0000264337 "Sinatra Reprise: The Very Good Years")
By the early '90s, the CD era had inaugurated a wave of box set reissues, and the 1990 Christmas season found Capitol and Reprise marking Sinatra's 75th birthday by competing with the three-disc [The Capitol Years](https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-capitol-years-mw0000971737) and the four-disc [The Reprise Collection](https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-reprise-collection-mw0000308941). Both went gold, as did Reprise's one-disc highlights version, [Sinatra Reprise -- The Very Good Years](https://www.allmusic.com/album/sinatra-reprise-the-very-good-years-mw0000264337). Sinatra himself, meanwhile, while continuing to tour, had not made a new recording since his 1984 LP [L.A. Is My Lady](https://www.allmusic.com/album/la-is-my-lady-mw0000691222). In 1993, he re-signed to Capitol Records and recorded [Duets](https://www.allmusic.com/album/duets-mw0000199181), on which he re-recorded his old favorites, joined by other popular singers ranging from [Tony Bennett](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/tony-bennett-mn0000006334) to [Bono](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/bono-mn0000771269) of [U2](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/u2-mn0000219203) (none of whom actually performed in the studio with him). It became his biggest-selling album, with sales over 3,000,000 copies, and was followed in 1994 by [Duets II](https://www.allmusic.com/album/duets-ii-mw0000124906), which won the 1995 Grammy Award for Traditional Pop Performance.

Sinatra finally retired from performing in his 80th year in 1995, and he died of a heart attack less than three years later. Anyone will be astonished at the sheer extent of Sinatra's success as a recording artist over 50 years, due to the changes in popular taste during that period. His popularity as a singer and his productivity has resulted in an overwhelming discography. Its major portions break down into the Columbia years (1943-1952), the Capitol years (1953-1962), and the Reprise years (1960-1981), but airchecks, film and television soundtracks, and other miscellaneous recordings swell it massively. As a movie star and as a celebrity of mixed reputation, Sinatra is so much of a 20th century icon that it is easy to overlook his real musical talents, which are the actual source of his renown. As an artist, he worked to interpret America's greatest songs and to preserve them for later generations. On his recordings, his success is apparent.

Biography") ### Lindsay Lohan Biography by [Heather Phares](https://www.allmusic.com/author/heather-phares "View more by Heather Phares") Actress/teen pop star Lindsay Lohan entered the world of show business at the tender age of three as a Ford model, which led to television commercials for the Gap, Pizza Hut, and Wendy's. She did more television work as she grew up, including stints on soap operas like Another World and The Guiding Light, as well as roles in The Bette Show and Get a Clue, a Disney Channel movie. Lohan's Disney connection, which included starring as the twins in a remake of The Parent Trap, continued into her teens and helped her expand her career into music: along with co-starring with [Jamie Lee Curtis](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/jamie-lee-curtis-mn0001070499) in 2003's Freaky Friday, she also performed the movie's theme song, "Ultimate." [![Speak](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0001354637/front/220/Qd_CZMdONf_rivVV9EUQFCpQg_7iAU1wjqLgK_xGXts=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/speak-mw0000263426 "Speak") The following year, Lohan starred in Confessions of a Teenage Drama Queen and contributed two songs to its soundtrack. Buoyed by these successes as well as her starring role in Mean Girls, Lohan hosted the 2004 MTV Movie Awards and won an award for Female Breakout Star. She also signed to [Tommy Mottola](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/tommy-mottola-mn0001228360)'s Casablanca Records, releasing her debut album, [Speak](https://www.allmusic.com/album/speak-mw0000263426), in December of 2004. The next year saw celebrity start to catch up with Lohan. While she continued her relationship with Disney, filming a remake of Herbie: Fully Loaded, Internet and tabloid rumors spread about everything from her health and love life (she's dating Wilmer, she isn't dating Wilmer....) to her late-night party habits and diva behavior. It didn't help that [Speak](https://www.allmusic.com/album/speak-mw0000263426) was less than a success. [![A Little More Personal (Raw)](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0000343099/front/220/N43uhAJi7os6CyNZknYiRwSijaXJlYnq0St31qpAJWo=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/a-little-more-personal-raw-mw0000260413 "A Little More Personal (Raw)") By the end of 2005 Lohan's persona as the wild and damaged teen siren -- whatever its ratio of truth to fiction -- had outshone her accomplishments as an actress and a singer. And it was into this caustic tabloid climate that she released her second album, [A Little More Personal (Raw)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/a-little-more-personal-raw-mw0000260413). Though the album was critically panned, it was certified gold early in 2006. Later that year, Lohan was switched from Casablanca to Motown Records by Universal Music Group. Though she focused more on her film career in 2006 and 2007 and continued to have a swirl of tabloid attention and media controversy around her -- including her arrest on May 26, 2007, for suspicion of driving under the influence and a subsequent stay at Malibu, CA's Promises Treatment Center -- Lohan planned work on a third album in the second half of 2007. ## [Lindsay Lohan Discography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/lindsay-lohan-mn0000831733\#discography "Lindsay Lohan Discography") Main AlbumsSingles & EPsAll Year (Oldest to Newest)Year (Newest to Oldest)AllMusic Rating (Highest to Lowest)AllMusic Rating (Lowest to Highest)User Ratings (Highest to Lowest)User Ratings (Lowest to Highest)Album Title (A-Z)Album Title (Z-A) | | Year | Credit | AllMusic Rating | User Rating | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [![Speak](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0001354637/front/120/Qd_CZMdONf_rivVV9EUQFCpQg_7iAU1wjqLgK_xGXts=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/speak-mw0000263426 "Speak") | 2004 | [Speak](https://www.allmusic.com/album/speak-mw0000263426 "Speak")

Lindsay LohanSantiago Felipe/Getty Images

[Lindsay Lohan](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/lindsay-lohan/) released her rendition of “Jingle Bell Rock” on Friday, 18 years after _Mean Girls_ solidified itself as a teen classic and tribute to Americana.

The actress shared the song as part of the soundtrack for her upcoming film, _Falling for Christmas_, which is set to debut on Netflix next week, right in time for the holidays. In the new film, the actress plays an unlucky hotel heiress with amnesia, who falls for the charming lodge owner. “Break out your \[camcorder emoji\] because yes, that is Lindsay Lohan singing Jingle Bell Rock in the Falling For Christmastrailer!” Netflix posted on Twitter.

While the Christmas classic was first released by Bobby Helms in 1957, the song made a memorable appearance in the 2004 comedy directed by Mark Waters and written by Tina Fey. Along with Lohan, who played Cady Heron, she was joined by fellow castmates Rachel McAdams, Lacey Chabert, and Amanda Seyfried in the film’s iconic “Jingle Bell Rock” scene.

Cotton](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/josie-cotton-mn0000284882 "Josie Cotton") ## [Kim Wilde Biography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/kim-wilde-mn0000103447\#biography "Kim Wilde Biography") ### Kim Wilde Biography by [Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://www.allmusic.com/author/stephen-thomas-erlewine "View more by Stephen Thomas Erlewine") [![Here Come the Aliens](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0004838767/front/220/AbRbt73LZXsp6aeig8Pet9_M69_UI9rrJSVvWL2-yAg=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/here-come-the-aliens-mw0003139677 "Here Come the Aliens") After starting out with a string of new wave hits in the '80s, Kim Wilde has proven to be equally adept at delivering high-quality dance pop and adult contemporary ballads. Those early singles were enduring classics like "Kids in America" and "Chequered Love," imbued with whip-smart toughness and new wave attitude, a position that gradually softened as she tackled more mainstream fare like her 1986 cover of [the Supremes](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-supremes-mn0000477875)' "You Keep Me Hanging On." Later records like 2021's conceptual [Here Come the Aliens](https://www.allmusic.com/album/here-come-the-aliens-mw0003139677) and 2025's [Closer](https://www.allmusic.com/album/closer-mw0004425474) see her return to the more daring approach of her early records with successful results, both in sales and artistic quality. [![Select](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0003467838/front/220/rsJS_0XMgPL7ORXfqLmC6ZhUoDg0hsvx4F4sL4oO-nA=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/select-mw0000845468 "Select") The daughter of '50s British pop singer [Marty Wilde](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/marty-wilde-mn0000375239), Kim began her own musical journey in 1980 when she signed with producer [Mickie Most](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/mickie-most-mn0000478992)'s Rak Records, releasing her first single, "Kids in America," early in 1981. It climbed to number two on the British charts that spring, while her second single, "Chequered Love," made it into the Top Ten; her self-titled debut album performed as well as her singles. The following year, "Kids in America" became a Top 40 hit in America, while [Select](https://www.allmusic.com/album/select-mw0000845468) kept her in the British charts. However, it wasn't until late 1986 that she had another U.S. hit with a dance cover of [the Supremes](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-supremes-mn0000477875)' "You Keep Me Hangin' On," which charted in the Top Ten on both sides of the Atlantic. In the intervening years, and for the rest of the decade, Wilde maintained a strong European chart presence, proving her longevity in the Austrian, German, Belgian, and Swiss markets. [![Close](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0000287313/front/220/KaESnInp3QtX1LbIdGN3q4Af7E_1E-2MlBBPmPAXRBU=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/close-mw0000652704 "Close") Wilde didn't have another hit in America but received a lot of radio play there in the summer of 1987 for "Another Step (Closer to You)," a duet with [Junior Giscombe](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/junior-giscombe-mn0001530214). Later that year, another duet, this time with the comedian [Mel Smith](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/mel-smith-mn0003707013) on a charity rendition of the [Brenda Lee](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/brenda-lee-mn0000934069) hit "Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree," reached number three in her home country, where it became a perennial seasonal record. Her 1988 album, [Close](https://www.allmusic.com/album/close-mw0000652704), brought Wilde further Top Ten singles across Europe, including "You Came," "Never Trust a Stranger," and "Four Letter Word." Her European tour in support of the record included dates opening for [Michael Jackson](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/michael-jackson-mn0000467203) on his [Bad](https://www.allmusic.com/album/bad-mw0000650293) world tour. [![The Singles Collection 1981-1993](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0000138341/front/220/7GofRU1Qs4ySmaB_1ZQ5Q4Af7E_1E-2MlBBPmPAXRBU=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-singles-collection-1981-1993-mw0000105257 "The Singles Collection 1981-1993") Wilde's commercial highlight of the '90s was a 1993 cover of the [Bee Gees](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/bee-gees-mn0000043714) disco track "If I Can't Have You," which charted high in no fewer than eight countries. It appeared on her first proper compilation, [The Singles Collection 1981-1993](https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-singles-collection-1981-1993-mw0000105257), and naturally, she embarked on a far-reaching "greatest-hits" tour the following year, taking in most of Europe as well as dates in Japan and Australia. Wilde's 1995 set, [Now & Forever](https://www.allmusic.com/album/now-forever-mw0000378905) failed to take off and became her last studio album for 11 years. She closed out the decade as part of a West End production of [the Who](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-who-mn0000577627)'s Tommy and married her co-star [Hal Fowler](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/hal-fowler-mn0001433363). [![Never Say Never](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0001280457/front/220/b3C47qdGapTRnxZs1i8beYAf7E_1E-2MlBBPmPAXRBU=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/never-say-never-mw0000773422 "Never Say Never") Early in the new century, Wilde took part in the plentiful '80s revival tours alongside regrouped lineups of [the Human League](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/the-human-league-mn0000895443) and [Five Star](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/five-star-mn0000796499). A 2003 collaboration with [Nena](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/nena-mn0000395187) on a bilingual version of the German artist's 1984 hit "Anyplace, Anywhere, Anytime" went to number one in both Austria and the Netherlands, and hit the Top Ten in numerous other countries, without seeing release in the U.K. Similarly, her 2006 comeback (of sorts) -- fueled by the EMI album [Never Say Never](https://www.allmusic.com/album/never-say-never-mw0000773422) \-\- took hold in each of the central European countries that had previously shown faith in Wilde, but it barely registered in the U.K.; in fact, after 2010's [Come Out and Play](https://www.allmusic.com/album/come-out-and-play-mw0002042248), 2011's [Snapshots](https://www.allmusic.com/album/snapshots-mw0002219489), and 2013's [Wilde Winter Songbook](https://www.allmusic.com/album/wilde-winter-songbook-mw0002584598) provided diminishing returns in Europe. It was a surprise when the quirky concept album [Here Come the Aliens](https://www.allmusic.com/album/here-come-the-aliens-mw0003139677) rekindled her career, hitting the Top 30 in the U.K. By 2021, Wilde was celebrating her 40th year as a performing artist with a lavish multi-format career retrospective titled [Pop Don't Stop: Greatest Hits](https://www.allmusic.com/album/pop-dont-stop-greatest-hits-mw0003528721). She also released a pair of collaborative singles, including "Shine On" with [Boy George](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/boy-george-mn0000771470). The compilation [Love Blonde: The RAK Years](https://www.allmusic.com/album/love-blonde-the-rak-years-mw0004173365) arrived in 2024 -- the same year she released the sparkling single "Trail of Destruction." It was the first teaser of her 15th album, 2025's [Closer](https://www.allmusic.com/album/closer-mw0004425474). The set, which touched on various genres she'd worked in over the path of her career, like new wave and synth pop, was produced by her brother [Ricky](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/ricky-mn0002683785) and featured daughter [Scarlett](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/scarlett-mn0002571098) singing on one track. ## [Kim Wilde Discography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/kim-wilde-mn0000103447\#discography "Kim Wilde Discography") Main AlbumsCompilationsSingles & EPsAll Year (Oldest to Newest)Year (Newest to Oldest)AllMusic Rating (Highest to Lowest)AllMusic Rating (Lowest to Highest)User Ratings (Highest to Lowest)User Ratings (Lowest to Highest)Album Title (A-Z)Album Title (Z-A) | | Year | Credit | AllMusic Rating | User Rating | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [![Kim Wilde](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0003467827/front/120/UeuvZ3YqhGPVkYYSEsTz3d_M69_UI9rrJSVvWL2-yAg=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/kim-wilde-mw0000202769 "Kim Wilde") | 1981 | [Kim Wilde](https://www.allmusic.com/album/kim-wilde-mw0000202769 "Kim Wilde")

Biography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/band-aid-mn0000116630\#biography "Band Aid Biography") ### Band Aid Biography by [Timothy Monger](https://www.allmusic.com/author/timothy-monger "View more by Timothy Monger") Charity supergroup Band Aid was formed in London, England in 1984 by [Boomtown Rats](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/boomtown-rats-mn0000520033) frontman [Bob Geldof](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/bob-geldof-mn0000801971) and producer [Midge Ure](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/midge-ure-mn0000479687). Intended to fund anti-poverty efforts in Ethiopia, the ensemble recorded the single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" for release during the 1984 holiday season. Aided by vocal efforts from [Bono](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/bono-mn0000771269), [Sting](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/sting-mn0000522377), [George Michael](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/george-michael-mn0000545074), [Boy George](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/boy-george-mn0000771470), Simon Le Bon, and a host of other contemporary pop stars of the day, the single topped the pop charts, becoming the number one Christmas single of the year and raising more than $24,000,000 for its cause. Such was Band Aid's success, several other celebrity-aided organizations launched fundraising campaigns the following year resulting in the star-studded Live Aid concert and the American charity supergroup [USA for Africa](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/usa-for-africa-mn0001775564). "Do They Know It's Christmas?" remains a popular holiday single and has been re-recorded twice by updated versions of Band Aid during the group's 20th and 30th anniversaries with proceeds again going to relief efforts in Africa. ## [Band Aid Discography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/band-aid-mn0000116630\#discography "Band Aid Discography") Singles & EPsVideosAll Year (Oldest to Newest)Year (Newest to Oldest)AllMusic Rating (Highest to Lowest)AllMusic Rating (Lowest to Highest)User Ratings (Highest to Lowest)User Ratings (Lowest to Highest)Album Title (A-Z)Album Title (Z-A) | | Year | Credit | AllMusic Rating | User Rating | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [![Do They Know It's Christmas?](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0005600578/front/120/g63AeoCklf4fLhN5d5hWvlWnbEN5fCjifro6xhIBuB4=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/do-they-know-its-christmas--mw0003673018 "Do They Know It's Christmas?") | | [Do They Know It's Christmas?](https://www.allmusic.com/album/do-they-know-its-christmas--mw0003673018 "Do They Know It's Christmas?")

# DO THEY KNOW IT'S CHRISTMAS?  by [BAND AID](https://www.officialcharts.com/artist/16510/band-aid/)

* * *

Band Aid's Do They Know It's Christmas? was inspired by a BBC News report on the famine in Ethiopia, Boomtown Rat Bob Geldof contacted Ultravox’s Midge Ure with a view to writing a song in order to raise some money, and assembled some of 1984’s top hitmakers into SARM Studios to record it.

Called Band Aid, the 37 performers at that point claimed 23 Number 1 singles between them, including Sting (with The Police), George Michael (both solo and with Wham!), Paul Weller (with The Jam), Paul Young, Phil Collins, Culture Club, Spandau Ballet, Duran Duran, Boomtown Rats and Status Quo. Also present were members of U2, Ultravox, Kool & The Gang, Bananarama, Heaven 17 and singers Marilyn and Jody Watley.

Do They Know It’s Christmas was rush-released on December 3, 1984 and entered the UK Official Singles Chart at Number 1 for five weeks selling over a million copies in its first week and claiming the [Christmas Number 1](https://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/every-official-christmas-number-1-ever-__3618/ "Christmas number ones") 1984 crown. It went on to become the second [best-selling song of all time](https://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/the-best-selling-singles-of-all-time-on-the-official-uk-chart__21298/ "best-selling songs of all time") in the UK, behind Elton John's Candle In The Wind '97.

The legacy of Band Aid has continued, with three subsequent sequels; Band Aid II in 1989, Band Aid 20 in 2004 and Band Aid 30 in 2014 each with a new group of pop stars, all three of which also claimed Number 1 in the UK.

"ZOMBIES 4: DAWN OF THE VAMPIRES [Original TV Soundtrack]") With her bright, agile singing voice, Freya Skye makes her own catchy, empowering pop music while also navigating work as an actor and singer in films, television shows, and video games. She was just 12 years old when she recorded her first single, the Junior Eurovision Song Contest entry "Lose My Head," in 2022. She starred as Nova in the Disney Channel movie musical [ZOMBIES 4: DAWN OF THE VAMPIRES](https://www.allmusic.com/album/zombies-4-dawn-of-the-vampires-mw0004579300) in 2025, the same year she released personal material such as the singles "Can't Fake It" and "silent treatment." The latter song was included on her debut EP, 2026's [stardust](https://www.allmusic.com/album/stardust-mw0004762563), which reached the U.K. Top 40. Born Freya Skye Jones in Buckinghamshire, England, Freya Skye began singing and acting at age five. Her first appearance on the international stage was at 13, when she competed in the 2022 Junior Eurovision Song Contest in Yerevan, Armenia. She represented the U.K. with her song "Lose My Head." Skye finished first in the global public vote and fifth in the official standings. At the time, she was a student at the Tring Park School for the Performing Arts. Around the same time, she began working as a voice actor in video games, including the English versions of Dragon Quest Treasures (2022) and Final Fantasy XVI (2023). In 2024, after signing with Hollywood Records, she released several effervescent pop songs, including "Who Says" and the bouncy seasonal outing "Winter Dream." She released more songs in early 2025 before appearing that July in the Disney Channel original movie [ZOMBIES 4: DAWN OF THE VAMPIRES](https://www.allmusic.com/album/zombies-4-dawn-of-the-vampires-mw0004579300), the fourth entry in the popular teen musical franchise. As Nova Bright, leader of the Daywalkers, Skye appeared on most of the songs on the movie's soundtrack, including "Snow Angels," Nova's duet with Victor ( [Malachi Barton](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/malachi-barton-mn0003936989)). She also took part of in the month-long North American arena tour Descendants/Zombies: Worlds Collide Tour. In addition to guest spots on TV's Wizards Beyond Waverly Place, back over on Hollywood Records, Skye released the song "silent treatment" before the end of 2025. It marked her debut on the Billboard Hot 100. In early 2026, she released her first EP, [stardust](https://www.allmusic.com/album/stardust-mw0004762563). With songwriters such as [Julia Michaels](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/julia-michaels-mn0002390968) and [Em Beihold](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/em-beihold-mn0004186337) chipping in on some of the songs, it reached number 35 in the U.K. and landed in the top half of the Billboard 200. ## [Freya Skye Discography](https://www.allmusic.com/artist/freya-skye-mn0004361731\#discography "Freya Skye Discography") Singles & EPsAll Year (Oldest to Newest)Year (Newest to Oldest)AllMusic Rating (Highest to Lowest)AllMusic Rating (Lowest to Highest)User Ratings (Highest to Lowest)User Ratings (Lowest to Highest)Album Title (A-Z)Album Title (Z-A) | | Year | Credit | AllMusic Rating | User Rating | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [![Who Says](https://fastly-s3.allmusic.com/release/mr0006359084/front/120/xm1734ShzaCLHN_rPN0vJZhUoDg0hsvx4F4sL4oO-nA=.jpg)](https://www.allmusic.com/album/who-says-mw0004271233 "Who Says") | 2024 | [Who Says](https://www.allmusic.com/album/who-says-mw0004271233 "Who Says")
